forecasts.label: Capital financing requirement
forecasts.note: Restated at each quarterly return. The Q4 restatement comes from the annual return itself, so it lands on the outturn by construction — the interesting movement is Q1 to Q3.

forecasts.label: Interest payable
forecasts.note: The council's own full-year forecast, restated at each quarterly return.

forecasts.label: Revenue spending (net current expenditure)
forecasts.note: The full-year forecast of net current expenditure — the running cost of services — restated each quarter against the same measure at outturn.

forecasts.label: Capital expenditure
forecasts.note: Total capital spending forecast each quarter (the capital payments return) against the annual capital outturn. Capital spending not met from grants or receipts is what turns into new borrowing, so a forecast running ahead of outturn is a borrowing signal.

in_year.label: Interest payable, as reported each quarter
in_year.note: Per quarter, not cumulative. The quarterly return is a lighter collection than the annual one and sums to roughly 92% of it nationally, so the two are shown apart rather than added together.

news_drafts.headline: Three Rivers forecasts £0.4m day-to-day overspend for 2026/27 and a £1.23m draw on reserves
news_drafts.lead:
Three Rivers District Council expects to spend £16.376m on day-to-day running costs (revenue spending) in 2026/27, £0.400m more than its latest budget of £15.976m, according to the budget monitoring report to 30 June 2026 (the in-year check of spending against budget). Policy and Resources accounts for the largest share of the variance at £217,000, followed by General Public Services at £178,000 and Climate Change and Leisure at £5,000. Supplementary estimates, extra budget approvals, of £0.272m have been requested.

The council's forecast sets net spending of £16,376,491 against income of £15,146,087 from council tax, government grants and business rates. That leaves a deficit of £1,230,403, to be met from the general fund balance. Deficits of £593,418 in 2027/28 and £642,913 in 2028/29 are also forecast and are likewise funded from that balance. In the General Public Services and Community Engagement Committee, forecast spending is £6.721m against a budget of £6.543m, a variance of £178,000, or 2.7%, after three months.

Homelessness shows a £120,000 adverse variance, which the council attributes to higher temporary accommodation costs. It is being met from the temporary accommodation element of the Revenue Support Grant, alongside grants of £329,704 for homelessness and rough sleeping and £108,733 for the Renters' Rights Act. At Watersmeet, an inflationary rise in the cleaning contract puts the forecast at £70,218 against a budget of £64,938, a £5,280 variance that is forecast to repeat in each of the next two years.

news_drafts.headline: Three Rivers forecasts £0.4m day-to-day overspend for 2026/27, with £1.23m deficit met from reserves
news_drafts.lead:
Three Rivers District Council expects to spend £16.376m on day-to-day running costs this year against a budget of £15.976m, an overspend of £0.400m. The figure comes from the first in-year check of spending against budget (budget monitoring), covering the period to 30 June 2026, reported to the Policy and Resources Committee. All three service committees are forecasting overspends.

Policy and Resources accounts for £217k, 4.2% of its £5.193m budget. General Public Services accounts for £178k and Climate Change and Leisure for £5k. The papers attribute the overspend mainly to changes in shared services arrangements with Watford Borough Council, under which temporary accommodation now forms part of the Revenue Support Grant, and to inflation on contracts. Within Policy and Resources, ICT charges are up £67k and HR charges £44k, reflecting higher charges from Watford. The elections contract adds £28.4k and office services £10.7k. The council is managing £74.9k of the variance by releasing budgeted contributions to money set aside (reserves), leaving about £142k not yet explained.

The council had budgeted for a deficit of £830,457 this year. The forecast is now £1,230,403, to be met from its general reserve, the working balance for its services. That reserve is forecast to fall from £5.18m to £3.95m, against a suggested prudent minimum of £2m. Deficits of £593,418 in 2027/28 and £642,913 in 2028/29 would take it to £2.71m by the end of 2028/29.

findings.headline: Property investment portfolio achieved 5.62% average yield, exceeding 5% target
findings.detail: The Council's Property Investment Board portfolio generated total rent of £1.049m against a total acquisition cost of £17.255m, achieving an average yield of 5.62%, which exceeds the original 5% target. The portfolio includes properties in Nottingham, Norwich, and South Oxhey.
findings.matters: The income strategy is delivering returns above target, demonstrating the council's property investment decisions are performing as intended.
findings.figures: Total rent due £1.049m, total acquisition cost £17.255m, average yield 5.62% vs 5% target
findings.quote: The total rent due is forecast to be £1.049m which will achieve an average yield of 5.62%, above the 5% target.

findings.headline: Capital programme includes £14.831m rephased from 2025/26
findings.detail: The 2026/27 capital budget was increased from the original £6.795m to £22.129m to include rephasing of £14.831m from 2025/26, primarily the Local Authority Housing Fund (£13.745m). This rephasing indicates capital schemes did not progress as planned in the prior year.
findings.matters: Large rephasing from the prior year suggests delivery challenges that may continue, affecting the council's ability to complete schemes on schedule.
findings.figures: Rephased from 2025/26 £14.831m (80% of total new budget), original budget £6.795m, latest budget £22.129m
findings.quote: The latest budget which totals £22.129m for 2026/27 includes the variances previously reported to Policy & Resources Committee in March 2026 (Period 10 Budget Monitoring) and approved at Council 14 July 2026 (2025/26 year end report). The forecast Year end position for 2026/27 is estimated to be £22.406m, which reflects rephasing of £14.831m from 2025/26.

findings.headline: General Fund balance forecast to decline from £5.181m opening to £2.715m by end of medium-term plan, approaching £2.0m minimum
findings.detail: The council's General Fund balance is drawn down by £1.230m in 2026/27 (from £5.181m to £3.951m) and continues declining to £3.358m in 2027/28 and £2.715m in 2028/29. The paper identifies a 'prudent minimum general fund balance of £2.000m' and notes reserves will remain above this level, but the declining trajectory leaves a narrowing buffer.
findings.matters: Depleting reserves reduce the council's financial resilience and capacity to absorb further shocks, with the forecast approaching the identified minimum threshold by end of MTFP.
findings.figures: Opening balance 1 April 2026 £5.181m, forecast 31 March 2027 £3.951m, forecast 31 March 2029 £2.715m, identified minimum £2.000m
findings.quote: A prudent minimum general fund balance of £2.000m is considered appropriate. The general fund balance is forecast to remain above this minimum level over the medium term.

findings.headline: Council tax and business rates collection rates declining year-on-year despite cost-of-living support
findings.detail: While collection rates are ahead of profile at Period 3 (Council Tax 30.2% vs 24.51% target, NNDR 30.87% vs 24.75% target), year-on-year comparisons show deterioration: Council Tax is down 0.1% from 30.3% at the same point in 2025, and Business Rates are down 0.76% from 31.63%. The paper cites ongoing recession risk to households and businesses.
findings.matters: Year-on-year collection decline suggests structural collection weakness that will flow through to the Collection Fund, impacting the council's spending power in 2027/28.
findings.figures: Council Tax 30.2% at P3 vs 30.3% at P3 2025 (down 0.1%); NNDR 30.87% vs 31.63% at P3 2025 (down 0.76%)
findings.quote: Year on year, the collection of Council Tax is marginally behind of the position reported at 30 June 2025 when 30.3% (-0.1%) of Council Tax due had been collected and Business Rates is also behind when 31.63% (-0.76%) of Business Rates due had been collected.

findings.headline: Council incurring disposal costs for recycling with no income recovery expected
findings.detail: The council currently faces costs rather than income from its recycling contract due to reduced global demand for recyclable materials. The council is being prudent and explicitly assumes recyclable income will not recover. The paper cites China's recession as evidence that demand will remain low for longer.
findings.matters: This represents an ongoing revenue pressure with no identified funding solution or mitigation plan, and the global economic outlook suggests the situation will not improve in the near term.
findings.figures: No 2026/27 figure disclosed; four-year graph shows monthly swings between costs of £20k-£30k and income peaks of £50k
findings.quote: Currently, the Council faces a cost to dispose of recycling as demand for materials has reduced. Recent economic performance data released from China, where the economy appears to have entered a recession, suggests that demand for recyclable materials could remain low for longer, increasing the cost to the Council.
